quests.passage: [Project Update: Customer Portal Launch] Hi all, a quick update ahead of Thursday's review. The portal remains on track for a launch on 14 October, but there are three points the steering group should be aware of. First, the payment integration passed testing last week, which was the largest technical risk. Second, the translation of help pages into Spanish and French will not be complete by launch; the vendor has confirmed that the Spanish pages will be ready on 21 October and the French pages on 4 November. We propose launching with English only and adding the other languages as they are delivered, rather than delaying the whole project. Third, our customer support team has asked for two additional days of training because the new system changes how refunds are processed. I have provisionally scheduled this for 9 and 10 October, which leaves no margin if anything slips. If the steering group prefers to delay by a week to allow time for the translations, I can prepare a revised plan, but I would need a decision by Friday to avoid losing our current testing slot.
quests.question: What does the writer propose regarding the translations?
options: Delay the whole launch until every translation has been finished
Cancel the Spanish and French help pages altogether this year
Launch in English and add the other languages as they are ready
Switch to a different vendor so the translations arrive sooner
quests.correctAnswer: Launch in English and add the other languages as they are ready
quests.hint: Find the sentence that begins "We propose".
quests.explanation: The vendor cannot deliver the Spanish and French pages by launch, so the writer suggests launching in English and adding languages later.
quests.evidenceLine: We propose launching with English only

quests.passage: [Room Rental Policy: Eastside Community Centre] The centre's meeting rooms may be hired by residents, local groups and, subject to availability, outside organizations. Residents and registered local groups pay the standard rate of $22 per hour, while outside organizations pay $38. A deposit of $50 is required with every booking and is returned within seven days of the event, provided the room is left clean and tidy and no damage is found. Bookings may be cancelled free of charge up to 14 days before the event. Cancellations made between 14 and 3 days before incur a 50 percent charge, and cancellations made with less than 3 days' notice are charged in full. Events involving alcohol require written approval from the centre manager at least 28 days in advance, and no event may continue after 10:30 p.m. Keys must be returned to reception within 30 minutes of the event ending. Groups hiring a room regularly, at least weekly for three months or more, qualify for a 15 percent discount on the hourly rate, but the discount does not apply to the deposit.
quests.question: A registered local group books a room weekly for four months. What hourly rate applies?
quests.hint: Apply the discount to the standard rate for local groups.
quests.explanation: Registered local groups pay $22 an hour, and regular hirers get 15 percent off, which makes $18.70.
quests.evidenceLine: qualify for a 15 percent discount on the hourly rate

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Choosing an Energy Tariff] When comparing energy plans, the headline rate rarely tells the whole story. A fixed tariff locks in the price per unit for a set period, usually twelve or twenty-four months, which gives certainty but may mean paying more if wholesale prices fall. A variable tariff follows the market: it is often cheaper when prices are stable, but your bill can rise with little warning. Many suppliers also charge a daily standing charge regardless of how much energy you use, so a plan with a low unit rate and a high standing charge can cost more than expected for a household that uses little. Switching suppliers is usually free, though some fixed plans charge an exit fee if you leave before the end of the term. Consider two plans. Plan A charges 24 cents per unit with a standing charge of 40 cents a day; Plan B charges 21 cents per unit with a standing charge of 70 cents a day. For a household using 10 units a day, both plans cost $2.80 daily, so they are identical. For a household using 5 units a day, Plan A is cheaper.
quests.question: What is the main risk of a fixed tariff?
options: Bills can rise sharply with very little warning.
Prices might fall while the customer is locked in.
The contract is always very short, often a month.
The unit rate is often hidden in the small print.
quests.correctAnswer: Prices might fall while the customer is locked in.
quests.hint: Think about what "locks in" means if the market price drops.
quests.explanation: A fixed tariff gives certainty but, if wholesale prices fall, the customer may pay more than the market rate.
quests.evidenceLine: may mean paying more if wholesale prices fall

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Regional Rail Pass: What You Need to Know] The Highlands Rail Pass allows unlimited travel on all regional services within the area shown on the map. A three-day pass costs $85 and must be used within a seven-day window, while a five-day pass costs $130 and must be used within fourteen days. Passes are validated on first use; the day count begins at that point, and each calendar day of travel uses one of your days regardless of how many journeys you make. Seat reservations are free on most routes but compulsory on the scenic Northern Line during summer, when a $6 supplement applies. The pass does not cover the airport express, buses or ferries, although holders receive a 20 percent discount on ferry tickets to the islands. Timetables vary by season, so check departure times before you travel. Children under 12 travel free with a paying adult, and up to two children are permitted per adult. Pass holders must carry photographic identification when traveling. Passes are non-refundable once validated, but unused passes may be returned within 90 days of purchase for a refund minus a $10 handling fee.
quests.question: A traveler validates a three-day pass on a Monday and travels on Monday, Wednesday and the following Tuesday. What happens?
options: All three travel days fall inside the seven-day window.
The pass can be refunded in full because a day was missed.
The third travel day falls outside the seven-day window.
The pass is valid for fourteen days from the first trip.
quests.correctAnswer: The third travel day falls outside the seven-day window.
quests.hint: Count seven days forward from the first day of use.
quests.explanation: The window begins on Monday, so it ends the following Sunday. The next Tuesday is too late.
quests.evidenceLine: must be used within a seven-day window

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Bike-Share Pilot: Summary of Findings] Over six months, the city's bike-share pilot recorded 41,000 trips across twelve stations. Usage was heaviest on weekdays between 7:30 and 9:00 a.m. and again between 4:30 and 6:00 p.m., suggesting that commuters accounted for most trips. Survey responses from 612 riders supported this: 58 percent said they used the bikes to travel to work or study, and 23 percent reported that the bikes replaced a car journey. However, the data also show a pattern that complicates the picture: stations near the university had three times the average usage, while two stations in the eastern district recorded fewer than ten trips a week. The report's authors suggest that the eastern stations may have been poorly located rather than reflecting a lack of demand, since residents in focus groups said they would use bikes if stations were nearer to bus stops. The report also noted that repairs kept about eight percent of bikes out of service at any time. They recommend relocating the two underused stations, extending the pilot by six months, and collecting data on cycling safety, which the first phase did not measure.
quests.question: Which finding best supports the claim that commuters made most trips?
options: The pilot recorded 41,000 trips across twelve different stations in six months.
Repairs kept about eight percent of bikes out of service at any time.
Stations near the university had three times the average amount of usage.
Usage peaked at rush hours and most surveyed riders went to work or study.
quests.correctAnswer: Usage peaked at rush hours and most surveyed riders went to work or study.
quests.hint: Look for evidence about both when bikes were used and why riders said they used them.
quests.explanation: Peaks matched rush hours and 58 percent of surveyed riders traveled to work or study.
quests.evidenceLine: 58 percent said they used the bikes to travel to work or study

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Opinion: The Trouble with Tipping] Tipping is often defended as a way of rewarding good service, but the evidence for that is thin. Studies of restaurant customers repeatedly find that the size of a tip correlates weakly with the quality of service and more strongly with factors that have nothing to do with it, such as the server's appearance, the weather, and whether the server introduced themselves by name. If tips genuinely rewarded effort, we would expect them to track it. Meanwhile, the practice shifts wages from employers to customers, leaving workers' incomes unpredictable and, in many places, dependent on the goodwill of strangers. Defenders reply that tips allow customers to reward good workers directly. But a system that rewards charm more than competence and leaves a worker's rent at the mercy of a quiet Tuesday is hard to defend as fair. Some restaurants have already experimented with an alternative, with mixed but instructive results. The alternative is not complicated: pay staff a living wage, and add a service charge to prices. Diners would see higher menu prices but would no longer be asked to run a payroll with their loose change.
quests.question: What does the writer argue about the link between tips and service quality?
options: It is weak, so tips do not reliably reward good service.
It is strong, so tips reliably reward good service.
It does not exist at all in any of the studies.
It depends mainly on what is on the restaurant's menu.
quests.correctAnswer: It is weak, so tips do not reliably reward good service.
quests.hint: Look at the verb used to describe the correlation.
quests.explanation: Studies show tip size correlates weakly with service quality and more strongly with unrelated factors.
quests.evidenceLine: correlates weakly with the quality of service

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Why Is the Garden Waterlogged?] The Maple Street community garden has a problem. Since April, the plots at the east end have stayed waterlogged, while the west-end plots dry out within a day of watering. Volunteers first suspected a leak in the irrigation line and had it pressure-tested; the line was sound. They then noticed that the east end sits about thirty centimeters lower than the west, and that a drain at the north corner is clogged with leaves and silt. After clearing the drain, water still collected at the east end, though it cleared faster. The group concluded that two problems were combined: poor drainage from the blocked drain, and the natural slope carrying water downhill during rain. Their plan is to clear the drain every autumn, to build raised beds in the three lowest plots so that roots sit above the waterlogged soil, and to install a shallow channel to carry surface water toward the drain. The garden's treasurer estimates the work will cost about $600, most of which will be spent on timber for the beds. They will review the results after the next heavy rain, since the cause may not be fully solved by these steps.
quests.question: Why did the volunteers rule out a leak?
options: The east end is higher than the west.
They never tested the pipes.
The drain was already clean.
The irrigation line passed a pressure test.
quests.correctAnswer: The irrigation line passed a pressure test.
quests.hint: Look at what they did first and what the result was.
quests.explanation: The line was pressure-tested and found sound, so a leak could not explain the waterlogging.
quests.evidenceLine: had it pressure-tested; the line was sound

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Why Is the Garden Waterlogged?] The Maple Street community garden has a problem. Since April, the plots at the east end have stayed waterlogged, while the west-end plots dry out within a day of watering. Volunteers first suspected a leak in the irrigation line and had it pressure-tested; the line was sound. They then noticed that the east end sits about thirty centimeters lower than the west, and that a drain at the north corner is clogged with leaves and silt. After clearing the drain, water still collected at the east end, though it cleared faster. The group concluded that two problems were combined: poor drainage from the blocked drain, and the natural slope carrying water downhill during rain. Their plan is to clear the drain every autumn, to build raised beds in the three lowest plots so that roots sit above the waterlogged soil, and to install a shallow channel to carry surface water toward the drain. The garden's treasurer estimates the work will cost about $600, most of which will be spent on timber for the beds. They will review the results after the next heavy rain, since the cause may not be fully solved by these steps.

To collect rainwater for later use
To keep plant roots above the waterlogged soil
To block the slope of the ground
quests.correctAnswer: To keep plant roots above the waterlogged soil
quests.hint: The purpose is stated in a clause beginning "so that".
quests.explanation: Raising the beds lifts the roots above soil that stays waterlogged.
quests.evidenceLine: so that roots sit above the waterlogged soil

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Leaving Your Home for a Month or More] Before an extended absence, a little preparation can prevent expensive problems. Start with water: turn off the main supply if no one will be present, and open a tap briefly to drain the pipes, unless your home has a sprinkler system or a boiler that needs water. In cold weather, set the heating to a low background level, around 10 to 12 degrees, so that pipes do not freeze; an empty house that is completely unheated is more at risk than one that is simply cheap to heat. Unplug appliances that do not need power, but leave the fridge on unless you plan to empty and defrost it, in which case leave its door slightly open to prevent mold. Ask a neighbor or friend to collect mail and check the property weekly, and tell your insurer if you will be away for more than the period stated in your policy, since some policies suspend cover for unoccupied homes. Finally, avoid announcing your absence on social media until you return, as publicly broadcast dates can attract burglars.
quests.question: Why does the writer advise a low level of heating in cold weather?
options: To save money on the heating bills
To prevent pipes from freezing
To protect the food in the fridge
To keep mold from growing on walls
quests.correctAnswer: To prevent pipes from freezing
quests.hint: Find the purpose clause after "set the heating to a low background level".
quests.explanation: A low level of heat keeps pipes from freezing, which is more important than saving the small cost.
quests.evidenceLine: so that pipes do not freeze

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [Reading the Ice] Deep in the Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets, scientists drill cylinders of ice, some more than three kilometers long, that preserve a record of the atmosphere going back hundreds of thousands of years. Each winter's snow compresses into a layer, and as it does so, it traps tiny bubbles of the air that surrounded the falling snow. By analyzing the gas in those bubbles, researchers can measure the concentration of carbon dioxide at the time the snow fell. The ice itself holds a second kind of clue: the ratio of two forms of oxygen in the water molecules varies with temperature, allowing scientists to estimate how warm or cold it was. The deepest layers are squeezed so thin that a single year may be less than a centimeter thick. Together, the two records show that carbon dioxide levels and temperatures have risen and fallen in close step through repeated ice ages. They do not, by themselves, show which change came first in every case, and researchers continue to study the timing. What the cores do establish is that current carbon dioxide levels are higher than at any point in the record, by a wide margin.
quests.question: How do ice cores reveal past carbon dioxide levels?
options: By measuring the thickness of each layer of ice
By counting the number of ice layers in a core
By analyzing gas trapped in tiny bubbles in the ice
By chemically testing the meltwater from the surface
quests.correctAnswer: By analyzing gas trapped in tiny bubbles in the ice
quests.hint: Look at what each winter's snow traps as it compresses.
quests.explanation: Snow traps bubbles of air, and analyzing the gas in them shows the carbon dioxide concentration when the snow fell.
quests.evidenceLine: By analyzing the gas in those bubbles

quests.instruction: Read the passage and select the correct answer.
quests.passage: [At the Repair Café] On the first Saturday of every month, the parish hall in Wenford fills with the sounds of screwdrivers and mild swearing. Residents arrive carrying toasters, lamps, bicycles with stubborn gears, and a cardigan that has met a moth. Volunteers, some retired engineers and some teenagers who simply like taking things apart, work at long tables, and the rule is that the owner must stay and watch. "We're not a shop," says Pauline Hart, who started the café four years ago. "If we just fixed everything and handed it back, people would learn nothing, and they'd be back next week with the same toaster." The café repairs about two-thirds of what it is given. When an item cannot be saved, volunteers harvest its parts, and a shelf by the door holds a growing collection of motors, plugs and switches. Donations are welcome, but nobody is required to pay. Pauline admits that the numbers are small compared with the amount of waste the town produces. "But a toaster that works is a small argument," she says, "and people carry it home."
quests.question: Why must owners stay and watch while their items are repaired?
options: For safety reasons, since the tools are sharp
To pay the volunteers for the time they give
To record each repair for the café's files
So they learn how to repair things themselves
quests.correctAnswer: So they learn how to repair things themselves
quests.hint: Look at Pauline's explanation of what the café is not.
quests.explanation: She says that if volunteers fixed everything and handed it back, people would learn nothing and keep returning.
quests.evidenceLine: people would learn nothing
